1: Nature and the person, the field and the knower of the field, knowledge and what is to be known: this is what I wish to know, Keśava.
2: This body, son of Kuntī, is called the field. The one who knows it is called the knower of the field by those who know these things.
3: And know that I too am the knower of the field, in all fields, descendant of Bharata. Knowledge of the field and of the knower of the field is what I hold to be knowledge.
4: What that field is and what it is like, what changes it has and what comes from what, and who the knower is and what power he has: hear this from me in brief.
5: The seers have sung of it in many ways, separately, in hymns of various kinds, and also in the words of the aphorisms on brahman, which are reasoned and settled.
6: There are the great elements, the sense of I, buddhi and the unmanifest. There are the ten senses and the one, and the five fields of the senses.
7: There are desire and aversion, pleasure and pain, the aggregate, awareness and firmness. This, in brief, is what is declared to be the field, together with its changes.
8: There is absence of pride and absence of deceit, non-injury, patience, uprightness, service of the teacher, purity, steadiness and self-restraint.
9: There is dispassion toward the objects of the senses, and no sense of I, and seeing the fault of pain in birth, death, old age and sickness.
10: There is non-attachment, no clinging to sons, wife, home and the rest, and a mind that always stays even whether what arrives is wished for or unwished for.
11: There is unswerving devotion to me, through yoga with no other, and keeping to secluded places, and taking no delight in a gathering of people.
12: There is constancy in knowledge of the self, and seeing the purpose of knowing the truth. This is declared to be knowledge. What is otherwise is ignorance.
13: I will tell you what is to be known, by knowing which one attains the deathless. It is the beginningless supreme brahman, which is said to be neither being nor non-being.
14: It has hands and feet everywhere, eyes, heads and faces everywhere, and hearing everywhere. It stands in the world, covering everything.
15: It appears to have the qualities of all the senses, yet it is without any senses. It is unattached, yet it bears all. It is without guṇas, yet it is the enjoyer of the guṇas.
16: It is outside beings and inside them, unmoving and also moving. It is too subtle to be understood. It is far away, and it is near.
17: It is undivided, yet it stands in beings as if divided. Know it as the bearer of beings, and as that which devours and brings forth.
18: It is called the light even of lights, beyond darkness. It is knowledge, it is what is to be known, and it is what knowledge reaches, seated in the heart of all.
19: So the field, and knowledge, and what is to be known have been told in brief. One who is devoted to me and understands this becomes fit for my state of being.
20: Know that nature and the person are both without beginning. And know that the changes and the guṇas are born of nature.
21: Nature is said to be the reason behind the making of effect and cause. The person is said to be the reason behind the experiencing of pleasures and pains.
22: For the person, standing in nature, experiences the guṇas born of nature. Attachment to the guṇas is the cause of the person's births in good and bad wombs.
23: The highest person in this body is the onlooker and the one who consents, the supporter, the experiencer and the great lord. He is also called the highest self.
24: Whoever knows the person and nature in this way, together with the guṇas, is not born again, in whatever way that one may be living.
25: Some see the self in the self by the self through meditation. Others see it through the yoga of sāṅkhya, and still others through the yoga of action.
26: But others, not knowing in this way, hear from others and worship. They too, devoted to what they have heard, do cross beyond death.
27: Whatever being is born, standing still or moving, know that it comes from the joining of the field and the knower of the field, bull of the Bharatas.
28: Whoever sees the highest lord standing the same in all beings, not perishing when they perish, is the one who sees.
29: For seeing the same lord standing equally everywhere, one does not harm the self by the self. From that, one goes to the highest goal.
30: And whoever sees that actions are done in every way by nature alone, and likewise that the self is not the doer, is the one who sees.
31: When one sees the separate states of beings standing in one, and spreading out from that alone, then one becomes brahman.
32: Because it has no beginning and no guṇas, this unchanging highest self, son of Kuntī, does not act and is not stained, even though it stands in the body.
33: Space has gone everywhere, yet it is so fine that it is not stained. In the same way the self, standing everywhere in the body, is not stained.
34: As the one sun lights up this whole world, so the owner of the field lights up the whole field, descendant of Bharata.
35: Those who know in this way, with the eye of knowledge, the difference between the field and the knower of the field, and the release of beings from nature, go to the highest.
